blocks.x: Yeah. We're recording today at 731 St. Peter Street. Yeah. What's today's date, Jerry?
You got me.
Here's the calendar. The 15th. April 15th. Pay your income tax.
Ides of April.
Alright, Jerry Bloomberg. Do you swear to tell the truth? The whole truth is nothing but the truth, so help you forward.
Right.
Okay, what's your name? Say it, so the secretary will know.
Jerry Bloomberg.
Okay. And what's your name? Mr. Wagner, what's your name?
I'm leaving immediately.

That's Bill Russell said that, and I'm Dick Allen. Okay. And I'm going to ask Jerry a lot of questions about Bunk Johnson and his style since you took lessons from him. That's the thing I'd like for you to summarize again is the things that characterize Bunk style more than anything else. I know that's hard to put into words you said on the last day, but I thought maybe you'd had some more thoughts since the last time. Don't let me interrupt you.
Don't forget about Dizzy style. Don't forget to introduce Bunk .

has a lot to do with his tone and his inventiveness, which you can only get a certain amount from records because a lot of it has to do with the element of surprise, and after you've heard a record once, you're no longer surprised by it.
Yeah, but didn't some of the aspects not come down on records?
Yeah, but those are the same things that you just can't put into words.
Well, you could hum some of those countermelodies, for example, like Honeysuckle Rose you said was really exquisite or something like that.
Yeah, he had a very good countermelody on that. I guess I could probably whistle a little better. Let's see.
Go ahead.
Let's see. That was a general thing, then he went into the release and so forth.
Did he play the release pretty straight?
Yeah, yeah. The rest of it was pretty straight. That was the theme of his countermelody on it.
Could you do it again, whistle it again? I want to hold the mic around here a little closer. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. .
Just something like that. But I thought it was kind of unusual. Sounds a little bit like the Lenny Tristano school or something. It was surprising to hear in that style.
You all said something about Dizzy as he was leaving.

Yeah, well, there was a story. Bunk one day said that he had just been up to the Apollo Theater where Dizzy was playing for a week. And he'd been listening to these beboppers. And he said that he asked Dizzy to define, if he could define his music. And he said Dizzy said he couldn't define his music. And so to this Bunk says, how can a man play music that he can't define? Of course, looking back on it, nobody asked Bunk if he could define his music. But it was kind of funny.
Do you remember any other little things like that that Bunk played that were outstanding that didn't come through the records?

I can't think of any that... Actually, most of the tunes he played to Stuyvesant were recorded eventually. I remember that on St. Louis Blues he played the four or five choruses that Louis plays on St. Louis Blues. Let's see.
Another thing I'd like to know is who came to the Stuyvesant?

Well, I guess there were a lot of young couples from around New York. I mean, most of the... I was just a visitor to New York and I didn't know too much about who these people were. There were some dancers from Harlem, from uptown, and people from the village, from Greenwich Village, who were interested in jazz. But there seemed to be... Most of the people just seemed to be young couples going someplace to dance, I guess. I mean, that might not... Maybe the first week or so it was jazz enthusiasts, but after that I think there were a large... There was a large number of dancers.
Would you see musicians, critics, celebrities there too?

Well, at first there were quite a few... Critics there. I think that kind of tapered off after a little while. I ran into Buckland Moon in New York recently whom I hadn't seen since the Stuyvesant days. I'm pretty sure I used to see him there often. Uh... Did you, uh...
Do you have any impression of Gene Williams or something I wanted to ask you about?

Well, Gene was a... a very bright guy. His initial, uh... impact, I think, was that of a kind of very well-educated, very polite, and somewhat shy, I believe. At least this was the first impression. Uh... With, uh... a kind of a sense of humor. I mean, he seemed to be, as I remember him, always on the pleasant kidding side. Although, uh... He might have been too much on that. I mean, maybe, uh... Maybe he was one of these people that smiles all the time, uh... regardless of, uh... how they feel, but, uh... Uh... He seemed to be a very, very, uh... pleasant fellow. At the same time, very intense about what he was doing, about jazz.
Well, there was a lot of this guy's hostility in this kidding?

No, I don't think, uh... hostility, but I don't think he, uh... I don't think he was a person who, um... showed how he felt at any particular moment. I think he was more, uh... one of us who wears a mask, you know.

Defensive kind of thing, in other words. Yeah, yeah. Just... It's always been interesting to me, uh... the musicians and the... uh... people who follow jazz, are constantly forced to put up this kind of defensive thing, I think, if you get involved in the thing.

Yeah, well, particularly with this kind of music, uh... you're open to a lot of ridicule, and, uh... there are always the, uh... the know-nothings who, uh... who give constant mockery at every effort to, uh... help the music along. I mean, I imagine bringing Bonk to New York probably exposed him to all kinds of... remarks around New York, so... Well, there's a lot of nudniks, you know,
who caught up with these 19th century ideas of progress. I think they ought to get up to date. Yeah. You know what I mean? Yeah. And they really don't look at things
in any kind of long view

or any kind of perspective. That's right. They really, that thinking is very much out of date. That's my belief, anyway. I'll have to put some of myself in there. One thing that interested me was... your description of the first time you ever came to the Stuyvesant, and you're approaching the place. Yeah.

What was the lie? Yeah, well, uh... first time I came, I was very young and kind of scared. It was the first time I was in a strange city by myself and, and, uh... I had received some kind of garbled directions of how to get at the Stuyvesant. And, uh, somehow I managed to... to get that, what was it? Second Avenue, I think it was on. But, uh... I remember, you know, wondering if I would ever find the place. And if I didn't, what would I do, you know? And, uh... Uh... I remember hearing the, the, uh, the music from a distance, just hearing, uh, bunk and baby as I, I guess, uh, crossed the street. I was probably half a block away from the, from the entrance of the Stuyvesant. And, uh... Uh, I could hear the trumpet and drums as I was approaching the place.
Well, that, by... My standards of present day New Orleans, that's not very loud, you know?
Well, I think maybe the, uh, the doors are heavier in New York and the walls thicker and so forth. Uh... But, uh, it was pretty loud. It was pretty loud. Well, say you're...

You know, when you're approaching Kid Thomas, did you have that experience of him playing across the street at Larry's place? And approaching that, it seems like you can hear him for further than any half a block.
Yeah, but...
But then he's playing right out into the open air.

Yeah, and, I mean, the doors were closed. This was in an enclosed, uh... I mean, when you walked into the Stuyvesant, you walked into a lobby, and there was a downstairs... There was a staircase, as I recall, and, uh, uh... Some kind of doorway straight ahead that I think went into the first floor hall. But anyway, as I remember, they were on the second floor, I believe, when they opened. And so you had to go up these stairs inside this lobby, and then, uh, you, uh, found the, uh, second floor hall, and it was kind of away from the street. It wasn't, uh...
You say Bunk played as loud as Kid Thomas does? You know, when he's playing at a peak?

Oh, I think louder. I think louder. Lighter than Kid Thomas? Well, yeah, I think Bunk had a more piercing, uh, uh, tone. I mean, it's hard for me to recall now, but he, I know he cut through. I know the band was a very loud band, and there were times when there was a lot of talk, and, uh, a lot of, there were a whole lot of people, there'd be a whole lot of people on the Stuyvesant, a whole lot of talk, and the band would be very loud, and Bunk would just cut through, uh, without, I mean, without any doubt at all. He just, uh, you'd hear every note anywhere in the place, just about.

I'm gonna just try to sort of jump around on some ideas. I hope it doesn't confuse you too much. But, you know, I'm getting them from Bill's former tape with it. What about Al Hanson? Did he give you any specific tips that he learned from Bunk?

I can't think of any offhand. Uh, thinking about tips from Bunk, though, uh, there was one discussion I got into with Bill Lofbrower, who apparently had been taking some lessons with Bunk, and he suggested, well, he was suggesting for me to, to move my lower jaw out, and I think that he said that Bunk had suggested this to him, or that he had noticed that Bunk was doing this also, uh, business of throwing the lower jaw forward, which, uh, I think Bunk did that to, uh, to a certain extent, when he played.
Did Bill Lofbrower have false teeth too? No.

You know what, maybe that had something to do with it too. No, I don't think it did, no. I mean, it's, uh, I think, uh, a lot of trumpet players have this underbite, uh, uh, and, uh, they play better if they can line up the lower jaw with the upper jaw, as far as the frontal plane is concerned, you know.
Now, I'm trying to think about some, like, uh, you notice some trumpet players, uh, maybe a little undershot, would hold their horn down, and Bunk would hold his very much out front, doesn't he?
Yeah, yeah, well Bunk would hold his up.
Yeah.
And I think, I think he had to push that jaw forward in order to be able to do that.
Uh-huh. Oh, I see. How often would you get up to New York in that period when you first went up there?

I don't remember. I think it was about, maybe two times during the first engagement, and maybe two times, the whole thing was probably, uh, well, it must have been more than that. I, I guess it was around seven or eight times, all together with the two engagements.
And then you moved...
For a few days each time, you know.
You moved up there later on. Later on, yeah.
Uh-huh.
What about the reaction of the crowd up there, to the music, uh, other than the dancing? What did they do?

Well, there would be a, uh, a large group usually standing right in front of the bandstand, which was, uh, pretty high up off the floor. I think the bandstand was about, uh, four, three or four feet up, off the floor. And, uh, maybe even more than that. Well, about four feet. And, uh, we'd all be standing there. I would be one of the, one of the crowd standing in front of the bandstand, and looking up at various, uh, idols, you know. And, uh, during a good deal of this time, there was, uh, dissension in the band. And, uh, actually it was kind of comical that there would be a group standing in front of Jim Robinson, who would be listening to him play his solo parts and so forth. And, uh, I remember there was a woman there who would turn around and sneer at Bunk, you know. Every time Jim played something real good. And I guess there were others that did the same thing back, although I don't remember that. But, uh, there were some, uh, animated, uh, uh, discussions on the part of the factions as well as on the part of the musicians. I remember going to a party down in the village during that time and, uh, got into a big argument down there over, uh, who was right in the band, you know. So, uh, it was quite lively.
What would they do at the end of the number? People, what would their reaction be?
Oh, usually applaud, I, I, yeah, I suppose.
They wouldn't scream and holler like they do to Indian Whistle and all that carry-on.
Oh, no, no, no.
People don't do that in New York.
No, this was, well, they probably do, but not these people. Yeah. This is a more, uh, wholesome group.
Well, who seemed to be running the thing, just from the standpoint of an outsider?

Well, I guess Gene was running it. Uh, uh, he had some kind of, uh, tie-in with the owner of the Stuyvesant, Mr. Menschel or something like that. And, uh, as far as I know, it was Gene that, uh, that engineered the thing. And, uh, later on, I think he went out and, and, uh, uh, did something similar with Kid Orrie's band, I believe. I know he was quite active.
What kind of guy was Gene? What kind of fellow do you seem to be on a pair? Again, uh, just seeing him.

Well, he seemed to be a very scholarly-looking guy, uh, uh, pleasant-looking, kind of, maybe slightly on the nervous side. Uh, uh, he wore glasses, uh, kind of thin-faced, I suppose. An ingratiating smile. Uh.
Anybody else around with him?

Well, he had a couple friends. I suppose, uh, when Bill Colburn was in town, they were together a good deal at the time. Uh. Uh, and, uh, Bill Russell was, uh, with him a good deal at the time, as I recall, at first, uh, I mean, I, I'm not, I can't remember clearly when one would leave town or the other, you know. Uh-huh.
It didn't interest you then, I guess, too much either.
Well, I was, I was, yeah, I was so, uh, that's, uh, trying to keep track of so many things. Uh-huh.
Uh-huh. Did you see many of the changes in the personnel that you, uh, around observed when one guy came in and watch the difference in the band?
Uh, the only guy I didn't get a chance to hear too much, as I recall, was Kaiser Marshall. I don't think I heard him. Uh-huh. I heard, I might have heard him one time.
Well, who was the first guy to leave the band, out of the original?
I guess it was Baby. I mean, I, I'm really vague on these things. Uh-huh. I'd say all I have is a, a bunch of impressions for the most part.
Did it make any difference?
Fragmentary, fragmentary. Oh, yeah, well, uh, definitely when Baby was playing well, I think that nobody could approach him. Uh, but there just got to be, uh, so much dissension there that, uh.
Well, Baby had his problems and Bunk had his problems.
Yeah.
Just like anybody else.

Uh. Uh. Yeah, so they, the only changes in personnel were, as far as I can recall, uh, uh, there were three drummers and two piano players. There was Baby, Kaiser Marshall, and, and, uh, Al Steele. This is, uh, the two engagements. Oh. And, uh, there was, uh, Alton Purnell and, and Don Ewell. Uh, there might have been maybe a third piano player sometime that I didn't know about, but as, as I recall, those, those are the ones.
Yeah. And who is Don Ewell?

Well, he's a piano player from Baltimore, uh, plays many, well, he has a way, uh, a style which, uh, uh, uses many of the stylisms, uh, uh, from the jazz tradition. And, and, uh, at that particular time, uh, he was very much on a jelly kick, and, and, uh, we used to stand behind the piano when he was playing with Bunk and, and just listen to the piano. He was playing beautiful jelly roll style piano.
And, uh, uh, well, specifically in the ensemble, what kind of thing would he be doing?

Well, he, uh, uh, basically was playing, uh, uh, a four beats to the bar, uh, things, uh, generally, uh, uh, I guess the same kind of part that, that, uh, Alton Purnell played, which is, uh, uh, uh, an octaves left hand playing, uh, almost a boogie woogie type figure, but just four beats to the bar, uh, going up and down a chord, uh, in the left hand. And, uh, in the left hand, and, and the right hand chordings around the middle of the piano along with it, and sometimes breaking up the rhythm, but the, the basic thing was this, uh, four beats to the bar, uh, identical, musically identical, uh, figures on all four beats, instead of being a two beat type thing, an umpah. Instead of being an umpah, he was a, uh, uh, studied figure.
That's it.
And, uh, uh, for his solos, he would play a stride style or a jolly roll style.
Do you remember any outstanding nights, uh, outstanding solos that really stick in your mind?
I can't remember the solos, uh, or, or nor the nights. I, I mean, I can just remember being dazzled, uh, many times.
Yeah, but I mean, an old thing like, you don't remember anybody particularly complimenting Don on something, or Bunk, or Bunk's attitude towards Don, or something like that?

Well, I remember that Bunk was very pleased with Don's playing, and, and used to get up from his seat and walk over to the piano and play a chorus with, with the piano, and just kind of get together with him, you know, so they could hear each other better, and, and, uh, uh, uh, uh, Bunk always had the best things to say about Don's playing. I know he always wanted to use them when he could. He called him his number one piano player.
Do you remember any favorite tunes that weren't recorded?

Uh, there was one that they used to play with, where they played with Don in the band that was never recorded, but I'm not sure. I think it was all alone on the telephone. I'm trying to piece it together now afterwards, uh, but it had a theme in it, uh, there's no place like home theme, and, and, and somewhere stuck in the middle of the tune. And, uh, I think it was some Irving Berlin thing, but it was real pretty. They, they really did it well. And, uh, outside of that, and Honeysuckle, and, uh, Mylenberg Joyce, I don't know if they ever recorded that or not. Did they record that, the punk record, Mylenberg?
Mylenberg, but not Honeysuckle, I don't know.
Not Honeysuckle.
What about the other New Orleans musicians up there?

Well, you mean, aside from Bunk's band? Yeah. Well, I, uh, got to know Danny Barker and Alan Nicholas, uh, while I was up there more than any other, uh, of the New Orleans musicians. Uh, played a few jobs with Nicholas and, uh, with Danny. Mm-hmm. And, uh, Pops Foster.
What do you think of their approach as compared with the approach of, say, the Joyce Lewis group, or with Lone Johnson's approach?
Well, you mean musically, or?
Musically.

Uh, well, uh, they had been around New York, uh, and more in touch with the day-to-day, uh, situations in music, uh, you know, more than, than, uh, these other fellows had. And, uh, and they, I guess had, uh, in their playing, arrived at more of a, a style that fits in with the New York scene, as well as, as, uh, their own, uh, tastes in playing. In other words, uh, Nicholas, uh, Nicholas, you know, can go into Ryan's session or wherever there's a New York session with, uh, any kind of swing musicians and play and fit in perfectly. You see, you know, um, if he had been down here the whole time or something like that and hadn't had this experience of, of, you know, doing this for many years, uh, it, it might, uh, it might be a clash, say. It might be more difficult to, uh, fit his playing to the New York. But anyway, I think this is, you know, one of the things about his style, uh, about Nick's style, although I consider him one of the great New Orleans clarinet players at any time, you know. I don't think he's, uh, I don't think he's lost anything, but I think he's, he, a bit more sophisticated, let's say. Uh. I'll say the same thing, uh, with Danny. Of course, Danny played, uh, with Cab Calloway for a long time. And, uh, knows modern harmony and so forth. What about Edmund Hall? Do you ever work with him? Yeah. I don't think he's lost anything, but I think he's, he, a bit more sophisticated, let's say.
Oh, did you ever work with him?
I just played one session with, uh, with, uh, uh, I like his playing very much. But, uh, I, I don't, really don't know too much about it. I mean, I haven't heard of him that much.
Well, what about Bechet's personal auntie there? What would you know?

Well, Bechet seems to be a very quiet guy, very difficult to get to know. He, he, uh, I think he kind of shut people out. I mean, that's the way, that's the impression I got anyway. Uh, because he's a very sensitive guy and, and often disturbed, I guess, with personal problems or, or who knows what. But, I mean, uh, he was, wasn't unpleasant. He, he wasn't, uh, insulting. He, or he didn't offend, offend, uh, anyone by shutting them out. But yet, he, he was kind of hard to talk to for me, and, uh, hard to get to know.
I guess Wilbur must have known him pretty well.

Yeah, yeah, Wilbur was taking lessons from him, and quite friendly with him. But I, I think he was kind of a reserved guy. When he talked, it was a slow, warm way of talking. But, uh, it was, I, it was just hard. I, I had a hard time getting to talk to the guy. Mm-hmm.
What about Mutt?
Mutt, I just met once. And, uh, uh, I really don't know. I didn't know too much.
You didn't hear him play too much.
I think, I just probably heard him once or twice, maybe, around New York, and his lip was kind of out of shape, you know.
Yeah. I've often wondered about Mutt on recordings, because he sounds like one of those guys, like Bunk and Bechet. Mm-hmm. That, maybe the recordings don't quite catch everything he had.

Yeah, well, he, Mutt did have a terrific presence. Uh, his playing didn't have the, the solidness that Bunk's had. Uh, Bunk gave a solid lead, something that everybody could hang on to. Uh, with Mutt, it seemed to be more up in the air, although he played beautifully. Uh, but the band was more on their own, as far as pulling, everybody was, had to pull together to get the thing going. But he also played a beautiful, tasty lead, and, and, uh, it worked. I mean, everybody usually did get together and, and, uh, produce something, produce a real good ensemble, you know. But Bunk, uh, was a much stronger individual, you know. And, uh, uh, he played with more authority. And, if, you can get the idea I'm trying to...
Yeah, I know what you mean. I know exactly what the difference that makes.
When he played, he was, he was boss. I mean, uh, and, if, if you, uh, were clashing with him, like, you'd have to find out what was wrong and take care of it, you know.
Do you remember anything about Mutt's vibrato?

Uh, I know, it was quite, uh, I don't know how he, uh, got it. Uh, I think it's, uh, Kid Thomas, I think, plays the horn very much like Mutt. I think, physically, I think they approach the horn, the production of tone the same way. And the vibrato, I think, is, is, uh, to me seems to be the same kind of vibrato.
Oh, ooh. Was, did you say Mutt was fast or slow?
Yeah, it was fast. It was fast.

The general sound of his horn is always fascinating me. I've always wanted to know how he got it. You know, because it's, it's a very characteristic sound. Yeah. Like, uh, Bonk's, or George Mitchell's, his characteristic, you know.

Well, I would say of the trumpet players I've heard down here, uh, as far as the approach to the horn, the horn is a little bit more than the horn is a little bit more than the horn is a little bit more than the horn.
This is Reel 2, Jerry Bloomberg, April 15, 1961. Okay, we're talking about the guys around here.
Yeah, well I was going to say that as far as their approach to the horns is concerned, I think that Mutt was very...

segments.title: Opening, date and oath at the recording
segments.summary: Dick Allen sets up the recording on St. Peter Street, jokes about the date and a mock oath, and says he will ask Jerry about Bunk Johnson's style.

segments.title: What characterized Bunk's style: tone, inventiveness, countermelody
segments.summary: Blumberg says Bunk's tone and element of surprise can't be fully captured on records, and whistles his countermelody on Honeysuckle Rose.

segments.title: Bunk on Dizzy defining his music; St. Louis Blues choruses
segments.summary: Bunk's story of asking Dizzy to define bebop at the Apollo, and Bunk playing Louis's choruses on St. Louis Blues.

segments.title: Who came to the Stuyvesant; impressions of Gene Williams
segments.summary: Blumberg describes the dancers, Village crowd and critics at the Stuyvesant, then Gene Williams's personality and the ridicule jazz fans face.

segments.title: First trip to the Stuyvesant; how loud Bunk played
segments.summary: Blumberg recalls arriving scared and hearing Bunk and Baby from half a block away, and compares Bunk's piercing volume to Kid Thomas.

segments.title: Jaw position and horn angle tips tied to Bunk
segments.summary: Blumberg discusses Bill Lofbrower's suggestion about pushing the lower jaw forward as Bunk did, and Bunk holding his horn up.

segments.title: Trips to New York, crowd reaction and band dissension
segments.summary: Blumberg gives how often he visited, how the crowd stood before the bandstand, the factional arguments over Bunk and Jim Robinson, and that Gene ran the engagement.

segments.title: Gene Williams's look and his companions
segments.summary: Gene as scholarly, nervous and ingratiating, often with Bill Colburn and Bill Russell.

segments.title: Personnel changes in Bunk's band: drummers and pianists
segments.summary: Blumberg recalls Baby Dodds's playing and dissension, and the three drummers and two pianists across both engagements.

segments.title: Don Ewell's piano, Bunk's praise, and unrecorded tunes
segments.summary: Don Ewell's Jelly Roll style and four-beat left hand, Bunk calling him his number one pianist, and an unrecorded tune the band played.

segments.title: Danny Barker, Albert Nicholas and New York-based New Orleans players
segments.summary: Blumberg played with Nicholas and Danny Barker and compares their more sophisticated New York style with the visiting New Orleans players; Edmund Hall brief.

segments.title: Sidney Bechet as a reserved, hard-to-know man
segments.summary: Blumberg found Bechet quiet and difficult to talk to, though Wilbur took lessons from him.

segments.title: Mutt Carey's lead, vibrato and tone compared with Bunk and Kid Thomas
segments.summary: Blumberg met Mutt only once or twice, says his lead was looser than Bunk's authoritative one, and compares his fast vibrato to Kid Thomas's; the talk continues on trumpet tone into reel 2.
